If we let $u=2x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

If we let $u=2x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\pi /6$ | $\pi /4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\pi /3$ | $\pi /2$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡u{|}_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{csc}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-\operatorname{csc}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(1-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
